title: Day 62 · Week 8, Day 6 — Myths: the scan cooks the baby and the Doppler should be refused, a fright or a row can end a pregnancy, and a positive on the booking bloods is a verdict
summary: The fifth Myths episode, closing Week 8 with the folklore of the first visit. Your baby is at the end of Carnegie stage 19 (about 18 mm): trunk straightening, head lifting, hands drifting toward each other over the heart. Myth one, the scan heats the baby: the half that's true (ultrasound is energy; the thermal index on every screen estimates worst-case warming, TI 1 ≈ 1 °C; the FDA caps output at 720 mW/cm² and MI 1.9), the thresholds (≤1.5 °C above normal 'without reservation'; 41 °C for 5 min is the hazard line; B-mode runs at TI well under 0.7, where BMUS sets no time limit, then a clock: 60 min at TI ≤1, 30 at ≤1.5, 15 at ≤2, 4 at ≤2.5), and the outcomes: the WHO systematic review (Torloni 2009; 41 studies, 61 publications) found no adverse maternal, perinatal, growth, neurological, cancer or cognitive outcome — only a weak non-right-handedness signal in boys (OR 1.26; Salvesen 2011 pooled 8,865 trial children, OR 1.15); Newnham's RCT (1993; 2,834 women, five scans with Doppler vs one) found more small babies (RR 1.35) and its 8-year follow-up (2004; 2,714 children) found identical size by age one and no developmental difference at any age; Cochrane 2015 (11 trials, 37,505 women) on routine early scans. The half-right part: pulsed Doppler delivers more energy, so WFUMB/ISUOG (2015) say no routine first-trimester Doppler, TI ≤1.0, 5–10 min; the FDA (2014) discourages keepsake scans and home Dopplers while noting no evidence of harm; the real home-Doppler danger is third-trimester false reassurance (Tommy's, Kicks Count). Myth two, stress ends pregnancies: chromosomal error is the largest cause of early loss (Hardy 2016, 40 years of karyotypes, rising with maternal age); the stress meta-analysis (Qu 2017; 8 studies; OR 1.42, 1.19–1.70; work stress 1.27) leans on a postal case-control asked after the loss (Maconochie 2007; 603 cases, 6,116 controls); the prospective studies split — Nelson 2003 (326 women, three scales plus cortisol, no association; stress predicted smoking and cannabis) vs Schliep 2022 (797 EAGeR women with a prior loss; HR 1.69 for any loss, 1.58 and crossing 1 for clinical loss); Nepomnaschy 2006 cortisol (emerging); shift work (Bonde 2013: fixed nights RR 1.51, 40–52 h weeks 1.36, 'reassuring'). The honest size: chronic months-long stress, never a fright or a row, and a 1.4× multiplier on this week's few-percent baseline (Doubilet & Guo 2024: 91.4% success after a normal early heartbeat, 93.8% without risk factors). Myth three, a positive on the bloods is a verdict: hepatitis B — vaccine 75%, vaccine plus HBIG 94% effective (CDC), tenofovir from 30 weeks for high viral load (Pan 2016 NEJM; 200 mothers; 5% vs 18% ITT, 0 vs 7% per protocol); HIV — <1% transmission with undetectable viral load (NIH), from 15–45% untreated; syphilis — penicillin cuts congenital syphilis 97%, stillbirth 82%, neonatal death 80% (Blencowe 2011); rubella non-immune — not an infection, <10 US cases a year since elimination in 2004, MMR immediately after birth (CDC); bacteriuria — antibiotics, pyelonephritis RR 0.24 (Cochrane 2019). Every screen exists because the treatment works.
action: Ten minutes tonight with the Day 61 file open to two pages. One: on the Day 55 Myths page, three new lines in your own words — 'the scan is sound, not radiation, and the trials with eight-year follow-up found nothing'; 'stress doesn't end pregnancies; chromosomes do, and that was decided on Day 14'; 'a positive on the bloods is a plan, not a verdict; ask when the plan starts.' Two: on the Numbers page, in the blank right-hand column, write the plan in four words or fewer beside each infection line before any result exists — hepatitis B: 'viral load, shots at birth'; HIV: 'tablets now, under one percent'; syphilis: 'penicillin, thirty days before birth'; rubella: 'MMR after birth, report rashes'; urine: 'antibiotic, repeat culture'. If the first visit is still ahead, add question fifteen to the Day 40 sheet: 'If anything on the bloods is positive, who calls us, and how soon?' If the results are in, read the right-hand column against the left and decide whether any line needs a call tomorrow.
